Subject: Re: Private runtime egress — TLS/SNI and audit artifacts

Alice — thanks, great questions. Summary below and I attached a compact checklist + the recommended IP export. High level:

1) mTLS: outbound connector -> control plane and telemetry endpoints use mTLS by default. The connector authenticates with a Redwood-issued client cert; the control plane enforces client cert validation and authorization scopes.

2) SNI: the connector sets SNI to a stable hostname (e.g., controlplane.rw-inference.com) per region. We provide the exact FQDN per region in the attached CSV so you can safe-list by FQDN+SNI in upstream proxies. If you must allow by IP only, see ephemeral IP section below.

3) Ephemeral IPs: Dedicated/private connectors may egress through a small, rotating set of NAT IPs. Rotation is orchestrated by our routing plane for capacity/maintenance. We publish the current IP set as an artifact and produce an audit log snapshot showing the rotation timestamps for any given day (sample included).

4) Audit artifacts we can provide today:
- ip-list.csv (current egress IPs per region)
- tls-samples.txt (subject/SAN and certificate fingerprints for our endpoints)
- rotation-log-sample.json (timestamped mapping of IP allocation changes)
- rdwd-egress-mtls-checklist.pdf (one-page consumer checklist, attached)

Next steps / questions for Aurora:
- Do you prefer SNI allowlisting (FQDN) or strict IP-only safelists? If IP-only, we recommend a short maintenance window that allows patching when rotation occurs; we can provide an SLA-backed rotation notice stream.
- Any procurement IDs we should reference on the artifacts (HubSpot or ticket)?

I'll hand off the technical detail to David to confirm the port ranges and header-level expectations.

Best,
Marissa

Quick technical clarifications from the runtime/ops side:

- Ports: outbound is standard 443 for all control-plane endpoints and telemetry ingestion. If you run deep inspection appliances that rely on port ranges, we only use 1024/ephemeral for internal sidecar comms; those are NAT'd behind 443 at the perimeter.

- SNI & Host validation: our client uses SNI exactly as Marissa described. The cert chain subject alt names include the regional FQDN and the leaf cert is rotated by us; we provide the cert fingerprints for your allowlist verification (see tls-samples.txt). Note: we do NOT rely on wildcard SNI beyond the documented FQDNs — please match the FQDNs we provide.

- mTLS detail: connector presents a client cert issued by Redwood CA; control plane validates both cert and expected CN metadata that maps to tenant id. Mutual auth prevents man-in-the-middle even if an egress proxy is compromised.

- Ephemeral IP rotation: we rotate at most once per 24 hours for production sustained workloads; emergency rotations may occur with prior notice. We publish rotation metadata and sign it for audit: {signature, timestamp, previous_ips, new_ips}. The rotation-log-sample shows a signed statement for 2028-07-24.

- Logging & evidence: we keep a 90-day audit trail of TLS handshakes for tenant connectors (SNI, cert fingerprint, timestamp, source IP). We can export a signed daily digest as CSV for SOC2 evidence requests.

Operational suggestions for firewall policy:
- Preferred: Allow by FQDN/SNI + verify cert fingerprint for outbound TLS connections.
- If IP-only: allow the exact IP set in egress-ip-list.csv and subscribe to our rotation webhook (we'll add you to the webhook feed).

I'll attach the sample rotation log and a snippet of the TLS artifact in the shared Drive link Marissa included.

-David
Principal Systems Engineer
Redwood Inference
